correctness.rationale: For the one-dimensional graph, each vertex contributes an incidence atom iff it has exactly one preceding neighbor. The 24 local orders produce precisely a six-cycle \(L\), a collapsible path \(U=C-A-E-D\) when both local hub-neighbors follow the hub, and two three-point sets \(W_a/W_c\) when the hub lies between them. Local orders can be globally interleaved around their shared hub. Thus the full complex is \(Z=L^{*p}\) with \(2p\) cones attached along \(W_{i,u}*\bigl(*_{j\ne i}U_j\bigr)\), with uniquely labelled apices. For \(p\ge2\) each attachment base has a collapsible U factor and is collapsible; cone/base relative collapses give an actual simplicial collapse onto Z, a PL sphere \(S^{2p-1}\). The \(p=1\) graph has eight vertices, twelve edges, and cycle rank five. Two executable finite implementations separately check the complete face decomposition, mod-two homology for \(\(p=1\),2,3\) and explicit free-face collapses for \(p=2,3\); integral and infinite conclusions follow from the structural proof, not the finite data.

value.rationale: A natural connected infinite graph family, square-cycle bouquets, exhibits a nontrivial transition: the full strong-Morse complex of a single \(C_4\) has five first-homology generators, but two or more petals simplicially collapse to single odd-dimensional spheres, dimension increasing two per additional block. The result supplies a uniform simple-homotopy theorem and explains exactly how the hub-constrained cones disappear; it is not a graph-by-graph computation, a mere substitution into the disjoint-union formula, or a known table recomputation.
